transgression: Tricks Zeus over the sacrificial meat at Mekone and steals fire for mortals
punishment: Bound to a pillar while an eagle eats his liver
notes: Earliest full account; links the theft to the origin of sacrifice and of women

transgression: Steals fire for mortals
punishment: Humans are punished with Pandora and hard labour
notes: Told to the poet's brother Perses inside advice about honest work

figures: Prometheus; Zeus; Hephaestus; Kratos; Bia; Io
transgression: Gives fire and skills to mortals against Zeus's will
punishment: Chained to a rock in Scythia
notes: Authorship by Aeschylus is disputed; the other plays of the trilogy are lost

transgression: Steals fire and technical skill from Hephaestus and Athena
punishment: Mentioned only briefly; the story moves on to Zeus giving justice to all humans
notes: Myth told by the character Protagoras to argue that civic virtue can be taught

transgression: Opens the jar and releases evils (as Zeus intended)
punishment: Humanity receives disease and toil; Hope stays inside
notes: Pandora is the instrument of punishment rather than the wrongdoer

transgression: None by the woman herself; she is the price of Prometheus' theft
punishment: Men must live with women as a 'beautiful evil'
notes: No name and no jar in this version

transgression: Not stated by Homer
punishment: Stands in a lake under fruit trees but can never drink or eat
notes: Odysseus describes what he saw in the underworld; the crime is assumed to be known

transgression: Steals nectar and ambrosia from the gods to share with his friends
punishment: A stone hangs over his head forever
notes: Pindar openly rejects the story that the gods ate Pelops at Tantalus' feast

transgression: Not stated by Homer
punishment: Pushes a stone uphill that always rolls back
notes: Punishment without a stated crime

transgression: Tells the river-god Asopus that Zeus abducted his daughter Aegina
punishment: Rolls a stone in Hades
notes: Later handbook gives a motive Homer omits

transgression: Attempts to assault Leto
punishment: Two vultures tear at his liver in Hades

transgression: Murders his kin and then tries to seduce Hera after Zeus purified him
punishment: Bound to an ever-turning wheel
notes: Pindar states the lesson directly at the start of the story

transgression: Boasts that she has more children than Leto
punishment: Her children are killed and she is turned to stone
notes: Achilles tells it to Priam to persuade him to eat despite his grief

transgression: Forbids worship of Latona and praises herself
punishment: Children killed; she becomes a weeping rock
notes: Roman reception; included for comparison with the Greek versions

transgression: Claims to be more blessed in children than Leto
punishment: Children killed; she is turned to stone on Mount Sipylus

transgression: Claims her weaving is better than the goddess's and refuses to yield
punishment: Turned into a spider
notes: No full Greek-language telling survives from before Ovid

transgression: Tests Jupiter's divinity by serving him human flesh
punishment: Turned into a wolf; his crime helps trigger the flood
notes: Jupiter tells the story himself to the council of gods

transgression: Sacrifices a human baby on the altar of Zeus Lykaios
punishment: Turned into a wolf
notes: Pausanias adds his own comment on why such stories are believed or doubted

transgression: His sons serve Zeus a meal mixed with a child's flesh
punishment: Struck by thunderbolts (the sons)
notes: Guilt shifts from Lycaon to his sons in this version

transgression: Their neighbours turn away the disguised gods
punishment: The neighbourhood is flooded; the old couple is rewarded
notes: Lelex tells it to answer Pirithous' doubt about the gods' power

transgression: Eats his guests instead of honouring them; Odysseus then boasts
punishment: Blinded; Odysseus' homecoming is delayed
notes: Two transgressions in one story: the Cyclops' and Odysseus' boast

transgression: Abuse Odysseus' household and mistreat the 'beggar' guest
punishment: All are killed

transgression: Takes his host's wife
punishment: Troy is destroyed
notes: The chorus names Zeus 'of guests' as the power behind the war

transgression: Boasts he is a better hunter than Artemis
punishment: Torn apart by his own hounds
notes: Cadmus warns his grandson Pentheus with this example

transgression: Accidentally sees Diana bathing
punishment: Turned into a stag and killed by his hounds
notes: Ovid says the fault was bad luck rather than crime

transgression: Two versions given: wooing Semele or seeing Artemis bathe
punishment: Killed by his hounds
notes: One source recording two competing explanations

transgression: Denies Dionysus' divinity and bans his rites
punishment: Torn apart by his mother and the women of Thebes

transgression: Attacks Dionysus' nurses
punishment: Blinded and soon dies
notes: Diomedes tells it to Glaucus to explain why he won't fight a god

transgression: Not clearly stated; he 'became hated by all the gods'
punishment: Wanders alone and grieving
notes: Glaucus tells his family history on the battlefield

transgression: Tries to ride Pegasus up to the gods' home
punishment: Thrown from Pegasus

transgression: Insists on driving his father's sun-chariot
punishment: Struck by a thunderbolt
notes: Theoi's Phaethon page must be checked; it may refer to a different Phaethon

transgression: Flies too close to the sun against his father's advice
punishment: Drowns
notes: No god punishes him; included as a boundary case

transgression: Ignores his father's warning and flies too high
punishment: Drowns

transgression: Challenges Apollo to a music contest (implied)
punishment: Flayed; his skin is displayed at Celaenae
notes: Herodotus reports the local landmark rather than telling the full myth

transgression: Challenges Apollo to a music contest
punishment: Hung from a pine tree and flayed

transgression: Loses a flute contest to Apollo
punishment: Flayed alive; mourners' tears become a river

transgression: Prefers Pan's music to Apollo's
punishment: Given donkey's ears

transgression: Imitates Zeus' thunder and lightning and demands worship
punishment: Struck by a thunderbolt; his city destroyed

transgression: Imitates Jupiter's thunder
punishment: Struck down and punished in Tartarus
notes: Part of the tour of the underworld's punished sinners

figures: Ajax son of Oileus; Athena; Poseidon
transgression: Boasts he escaped the sea despite the gods
punishment: Drowned
notes: Proteus reports it to Menelaus; the boast is the immediate cause

transgression: Tells Athena he does not need divine help
punishment: Driven mad; later kills himself
notes: A messenger reports the prophet Calchas' explanation

transgression: Kills a stag in Artemis' grove and boasts
punishment: The fleet is held at Aulis until Iphigenia is sacrificed
notes: Electra uses it to defend her father against Clytemnestra

transgression: Brings a dead man back to life for gold
punishment: Killed by a thunderbolt

transgression: Sleeps with a mortal while pregnant by Apollo
punishment: Killed; her son Asclepius is saved from the pyre

transgression: Rejects Aphrodite and sexual love
punishment: Killed after his father's curse
notes: Aphrodite announces the punishment in the opening speech

transgression: Boasts he could beat the Muses in song
punishment: Maimed and loses his gift of song

transgression: Is loved by a goddess (Eos)
punishment: Shot by Artemis
notes: Calypso uses it to complain that the gods resent goddesses with mortal lovers

transgression: Attempts to assault Opis or challenges Artemis at the discus
punishment: Killed
notes: Several versions listed side by side

transgression: Cuts down Demeter's sacred grove
punishment: Endless hunger
notes: The hymn is set during a festival procession for Demeter

transgression: Cuts down Ceres' sacred oak
punishment: Insatiable hunger; he eats himself

transgression: Boasts she is more beautiful than the Nereids
punishment: A flood and a sea-monster; her daughter is offered to it
notes: Theoi covers this on a Perseus page rather than a Cassiopeia page

transgression: Oeneus forgets to sacrifice to Artemis
punishment: Sends the Calydonian boar
notes: Phoenix tells it to persuade Achilles to accept the gifts and fight

transgression: Refuses to pay the gods their agreed wage
punishment: Threats now; Troy's later troubles
notes: Poseidon reminds Apollo of it to argue they should not help Troy

transgression: Challenges Apollo at archery
punishment: Killed young
notes: Odysseus uses it to say he will not compete with the heroes of old

transgression: Try to pile mountains up to reach heaven
punishment: Killed before they reach manhood

transgression: Eat the sacred cattle of the Sun despite warnings
punishment: Shipwrecked and drowned
notes: The poem's opening (1.6–9) already names this as their own recklessness

transgression: Seduces Clytemnestra and kills Agamemnon despite a warning
punishment: Killed by Orestes
notes: Zeus uses the case to argue that humans cause their own suffering

transgression: Keeps the bull he promised to sacrifice to Poseidon
punishment: His wife is made to desire the bull; the Minotaur is born

transgression: Forgets to sacrifice to Artemis at his wedding
punishment: Finds his bridal chamber full of snakes

transgression: Call themselves Zeus and Hera
punishment: Turned into birds

transgression: None: Ceyx dies in a shipwreck
punishment: Both become kingfishers
notes: The same couple without any crime; a love story instead of a warning

transgression: None by Io; she is loved by Zeus
punishment: Turned into a cow and chased by a gadfly
notes: Io is a victim; included to show that 'punishment' does not always mean guilt

transgression: Becomes pregnant by Jupiter and hides it from Diana
punishment: Turned into a bear; later made a constellation

transgression: Loses her virginity (to Zeus)
punishment: Turned into a bear and shot
notes: Apollodorus lists which earlier authors blame which goddess

transgression: Scorns everyone who loves him
punishment: Falls in love with his reflection and wastes away

transgression: Keep weaving instead of joining Bacchus' festival
punishment: Turned into bats
notes: The sisters tell each other stories while they work; the stories form most of the episode

transgression: Refuse to join the Bacchic rites
punishment: Driven mad; turned into night birds

figures: the daughters of Proetus; Hera; Artemis
transgression: Mock Hera's temple and boast of their father's wealth
punishment: Driven mad until Artemis heals them
notes: The story ends by founding an altar and rites for Artemis

figures: Er; Ardiaeus; the judges of the dead
transgression: Live unjustly (e.g. the tyrant Ardiaeus)
punishment: Repaid tenfold; incurable tyrants are kept in Tartarus
notes: Socrates closes the Republic's argument about justice with this story

transgression: Kills his father and marries his mother without knowing
punishment: Blinds himself and goes into exile
notes: Whether this is a story of guilt and punishment at all is a long-running debate

transgression: Demands gold from Mercury and blocks his way to her sister
punishment: Infected with envy and turned to stone

transgression: Atreus serves Thyestes his own children
punishment: The curse falls on Agamemnon's house
notes: Aegisthus tells it to justify killing Agamemnon
